about: Every voiced line of the chapter's ink: who speaks it, the exact words shown on the page ("text"), and what the voice is given ("say": the same words with eleven_v3 audio tags). tools/lines.mjs --check voices.json proves "text" matches the ink; tools/directions.py writes this file. Each line has "takes" takes, media/vo/<id>-1.mp3 and so on, and one more if its id is in "secondTake"; the page plays one at random.

call-coroner-1.speaker: narrator
call-coroner-1.text: You phone the coroner at home. He is in his garden; you can hear a mower stop.
call-coroner-1.say: [quiet, observant] You phone the coroner at home. He is in his garden; you can hear a mower stop.

call-coroner-2.speaker: ros
call-coroner-2.text: The deceased drowned. He has a bruise on the head that Dr Shah can't measure yet.
call-coroner-2.say: [calm, plain] The deceased drowned. He has a bruise on the head that Dr Shah can't measure yet.

call-coroner-3.speaker: ros
call-coroner-3.text: If he was knocked out, it's an accident. If he was awake, someone has to explain the water.
call-coroner-3.say: [calm, plain] If he was knocked out, it's an accident. If he was awake, someone has to explain the water.

call-coroner-4.speaker: ros
call-coroner-4.text: I'd like a forensic post-mortem. Before the body is released.
call-coroner-4.say: [calm, plain] I'd like a forensic post-mortem. Before the body is released.

call-coroner-5.speaker: coroner
call-coroner-5.text: The funeral's booked for Wednesday, Ros.
call-coroner-5.say: [weary, kind] The funeral's booked for Wednesday, Ros.

call-coroner-7.speaker: coroner
call-coroner-7.text: All right. Dr Shah can do it tomorrow morning. Someone had better tell Mrs Strand before the undertaker does.
call-coroner-7.say: [weary, kind] All right. Dr Shah can do it tomorrow morning. Someone had better tell Mrs Strand before the undertaker does.

end-accident-1.speaker: narrator
end-accident-1.text: Quaile closes the folder and gives it back to you.
end-accident-1.say: [quiet, observant] Quaile closes the folder and gives it back to you.

end-accident-2.speaker: narrator
end-accident-2.text: The coroner records an accident. At the funeral Clive Amory gives the address. Kit Rowe stands at the back, in her lock-keeper's fleece.
end-accident-2.say: [quiet, observant] The coroner records an accident. At the funeral Clive Amory gives the address. Kit Rowe stands at the back, in her lock-keeper's fleece.

end-full-1.speaker: narrator
end-full-1.text: Quaile takes the folder. At four o'clock she rings you.
end-full-1.say: [quiet, observant] Quaile takes the folder. At four o'clock she rings you.

end-full-2.speaker: quaile
end-full-2.text: He's asked to speak to you. Not to me. You can say no.
end-full-2.say: [drily] He's asked to speak to you. Not to me. You can say no.

end-full-3.speaker: narrator
end-full-3.text: In the interview room Clive Amory has his reading glasses on, and a solicitor beside him who has stopped writing.
end-full-3.say: [quiet, observant] In the interview room Clive Amory has his reading glasses on, and a solicitor beside him who has stopped writing.

end-full-4.speaker: clive
end-full-4.text: I put the reserve into the Meridian fund on Ted Hollins's advice, and when it closed I told the committee nothing, because I thought I could put it right before anyone needed the money.
end-full-4.say: [quiet, steady] I put the reserve into the Meridian fund on Ted Hollins's advice, and when it closed I told the committee nothing, because I thought I could put it right before anyone needed the money.

end-full-5.speaker: clive
end-full-5.text: When he fell I could hear him, and I went to the car for my windlass, and I wound the paddles up; when it was full I wound them down and put the chain back on, because that is what you do at night.
end-full-5.say: [very quiet] When he fell I could hear him, and I went to the car for my windlass, and I wound the paddles up; when it was full I wound them down and put the chain back on, because that is what you do at night.

end-full-6.speaker: clive
end-full-6.text: Ted gave the parish council the same advice about Meridian, and he has made gates for four other trusts since nineteen ninety. You might ask how many of those were new.
end-full-6.say: [gentle, precise] Ted gave the parish council the same advice about Meridian, and he has made gates for four other trusts since nineteen ninety. You might ask how many of those were new.

end-full-7.speaker: clive
end-full-7.text: Neville was right about the gates.
end-full-7.say: [long pause] [almost a whisper] Neville was right about the gates.

end-half-1.speaker: quaile
end-half-1.text: This is a fraud, Mrs Kettering. I'll pass it on.
end-half-1.say: [drily] This is a fraud, Mrs Kettering. I'll pass it on.

end-half-3.speaker: narrator
end-half-3.text: Clive Amory's solicitor takes the push apart in an hour. Nobody saw a push, and nothing in the file shows one.
end-half-3.say: [quiet, observant] Clive Amory's solicitor takes the push apart in an hour. Nobody saw a push, and nothing in the file shows one.

end-half-4.speaker: narrator
end-half-4.text: The file names the right man and cannot say what he did. Clive's solicitor asks for the evidence on the chain and the water, and there is not enough.
end-half-4.say: [quiet, observant] The file names the right man and cannot say what he did. Clive's solicitor asks for the evidence on the chain and the water, and there is not enough.

end-half-5.speaker: narrator
end-half-5.text: In the spring Clive Amory pleads guilty to fraud over the gate grant, and pays it back, and says in court that the chairman was the best friend the canal ever had.
end-half-5.say: [quiet, observant] In the spring Clive Amory pleads guilty to fraud over the gate grant, and pays it back, and says in court that the chairman was the best friend the canal ever had.

end-open-1.speaker: narrator
end-open-1.text: Quaile closes the folder and gives it back to you.
end-open-1.say: [quiet, observant] Quaile closes the folder and gives it back to you.

end-open-2.speaker: narrator
end-open-2.text: The coroner records an open conclusion. In November Annette Strand writes to you: one page, in a teacher's hand. She asks what happened in the last hour.
end-open-2.say: [quiet, observant] The coroner records an open conclusion. In November Annette Strand writes to you: one page, in a teacher's hand. She asks what happened in the last hour.

end-thin-2.speaker: narrator
end-thin-2.text: On Wednesday Neville Strand is cremated, as booked.
end-thin-2.say: [quiet, observant] On Wednesday Neville Strand is cremated, as booked.

end-thin-3.speaker: narrator
end-thin-3.text: In January Clive Amory's solicitor tells a judge that a man with a head injury can drown in half a metre of water, and there is no second post-mortem to say otherwise. Clive is convicted of fraud, and of perverting the course of justice for what he told you. He serves fourteen months.
end-thin-3.say: [quiet, observant] In January Clive Amory's solicitor tells a judge that a man with a head injury can drown in half a metre of water, and there is no second post-mortem to say otherwise. Clive is convicted of fraud, and of perverting the course of justice for what he told you. He serves fourteen months.

end-thin-4.speaker: narrator
end-thin-4.text: In February Annette writes to ask for a copy of your report.
end-thin-4.say: [quiet, observant] In February Annette writes to ask for a copy of your report.

end-wrong-1.speaker: narrator
end-wrong-1.text: Quaile reads your file again and takes it.
end-wrong-1.say: [quiet, observant] Quaile reads your file again and takes it.

end-wrong-2.speaker: narrator
end-wrong-2.text: The van Dams are stopped at Harwich with their car on the ferry. They are held for two days and released without charge. Maaike sends you all of her photographs from the holiday, eighty-one of them, with no message.
end-wrong-2.say: [quiet, observant] The van Dams are stopped at Harwich with their car on the ferry. They are held for two days and released without charge. Maaike sends you all of her photographs from the holiday, eighty-one of them, with no message.

end-wrong-3.speaker: narrator
end-wrong-3.text: Kit Rowe is interviewed under caution on Tuesday. On Wednesday the Harbour in Bristol withdraws its offer. On Thursday the committee ends her post, as Neville proposed. Clive Amory writes her a reference.
end-wrong-3.say: [quiet, observant] Kit Rowe is interviewed under caution on Tuesday. On Wednesday the Harbour in Bristol withdraws its offer. On Thursday the committee ends her post, as Neville proposed. Clive Amory writes her a reference.

end-wrong-4.speaker: narrator
end-wrong-4.text: Clive Amory keeps the trust's accounts.
end-wrong-4.say: [quiet, observant] Clive Amory keeps the trust's accounts.

evening-1.speaker: narrator
evening-1.text: At eight the phone rings. Dr Shah, from a station platform.
evening-1.say: [quiet, observant] At eight the phone rings. Dr Shah, from a station platform.

evening-2.speaker: shah
evening-2.text: Second post-mortem. The bruise on the head is slight. No fracture, no bleeding inside the skull. He was conscious.
evening-2.say: [brisk, clinical] Second post-mortem. The bruise on the head is slight. No fracture, no bleeding inside the skull. He was conscious.

evening-3.speaker: shah
evening-3.text: The nails on both hands are torn, with brick in them. He tried to climb the chamber wall. The broken thigh bled into the muscle for some minutes before he died.
evening-3.say: [brisk, clinical] The nails on both hands are torn, with brick in them. He tried to climb the chamber wall. The broken thigh bled into the muscle for some minutes before he died.

evening-4.speaker: shah
evening-4.text: Plainly: a conscious man with a broken leg can sit up in half a metre of water. He drowned because the water got deeper.
evening-4.say: [brisk, clinical] Plainly: a conscious man with a broken leg can sit up in half a metre of water. He drowned because the water got deeper.

p1-1.speaker: narrator
p1-1.text: Lock fourteen of the Wyke Arm. Friday, nine in the morning.
p1-1.say: [quiet, observant] Lock fourteen of the Wyke Arm. Friday, nine in the morning.

p1-2.speaker: narrator
p1-2.text: You are Ros Kettering, coroner's officer for the county. A sudden death comes to you before it goes to the coroner. You retire in March.
p1-2.say: [quiet, observant] You are Ros Kettering, coroner's officer for the county. A sudden death comes to you before it goes to the coroner. You retire in March.

p1-3.speaker: narrator
p1-3.text: The police tape runs from a balance beam to a fence post. The body went to the mortuary an hour ago. Neville Strand, sixty-six, chairman of the canal trust. Found at ten past seven by the crew of a hire boat.
p1-3.say: [quiet, observant] The police tape runs from a balance beam to a fence post. The body went to the mortuary an hour ago. Neville Strand, sixty-six, chairman of the canal trust. Found at ten past seven by the crew of a hire boat.

p1-4.speaker: narrator
p1-4.text: The lock is full to the top of the gates. Below thirteen you can see the hire boat that came down the flight last night, moored.
p1-4.say: [quiet, observant] The lock is full to the top of the gates. Below thirteen you can see the hire boat that came down the flight last night, moored.

p1-5.speaker: narrator
p1-5.text: A man in a trust fleece waits by the top gate with two coffees.
p1-5.say: [quiet, observant] A man in a trust fleece waits by the top gate with two coffees.

p1-bag-1.speaker: narrator
p1-bag-1.text: A police exhibit bag lies on the lockside. In it is a windlass: an iron handle, bent in an L, for winding paddles. A plastic tag on it says WREN, and the name of the hire company.
p1-bag-1.say: [quiet, observant] A police exhibit bag lies on the lockside. In it is a windlass: an iron handle, bent in an L, for winding paddles. A plastic tag on it says WREN, and the name of the hire company.

p1-bag-2.speaker: narrator
p1-bag-2.text: A constable lifts the tape for you.
p1-bag-2.say: [quiet, observant] A constable lifts the tape for you.

p1-bag-3.speaker: constable
p1-bag-3.text: It was by the top gate, ma'am. It's off the hire boat. Dutch couple. They came down through the locks last night and found him this morning.
p1-bag-3.say: [polite] It was by the top gate, ma'am. It's off the hire boat. Dutch couple. They came down through the locks last night and found him this morning.

p1-clive-1.speaker: clive
p1-clive-1.text: Anything else I can tell you, Mrs Kettering?
p1-clive-1.say: [gentle, precise] Anything else I can tell you, Mrs Kettering?

p1-clive-10.speaker: clive
p1-clive-10.text: At night we chain the paddle gear, to save water. The chairman did it on his walk. Every night at ten.
p1-clive-10.say: [gentle, precise] At night we chain the paddle gear, to save water. The chairman did it on his walk. Every night at ten.

p1-clive-11.speaker: ros
p1-clive-11.text: When did you last speak to the deceased?
p1-clive-11.say: [calm, plain] When did you last speak to the deceased?

p1-clive-12.speaker: clive
p1-clive-12.text: He rang me at five to eleven last night, about the minutes of our meeting. I told him to ring me in the morning, and I went to bed.
p1-clive-12.say: [gentle, precise] He rang me at five to eleven last night, about the minutes of our meeting. I told him to ring me in the morning, and I went to bed.

p1-clive-13.speaker: narrator
p1-clive-13.text: His car is in the lock car park: a green estate with a trust sticker in the back window.
p1-clive-13.say: [quiet, observant] His car is in the lock car park: a green estate with a trust sticker in the back window.

p1-clive-2.speaker: clive
p1-clive-2.text: Mrs Kettering? Clive Amory. I'm the trust's treasurer. Kit's away, so I said I'd meet you. White, no sugar. I guessed.
p1-clive-2.say: [gentle, precise] Mrs Kettering? Clive Amory. I'm the trust's treasurer. Kit's away, so I said I'd meet you. White, no sugar. I guessed.

p1-clive-3.speaker: ros
p1-clive-3.text: Thank you. You knew him well.
p1-clive-3.say: [calm, plain] Thank you. You knew him well.

p1-clive-4.speaker: clive
p1-clive-4.text: Fourteen years on the committee with the chairman.
p1-clive-4.say: [gentle, precise] Fourteen years on the committee with the chairman.

p1-clive-5.speaker: narrator
p1-clive-5.text: He has a windlass in his fleece pocket, and he holds the coffee with both hands.
p1-clive-5.say: [quiet, observant] He has a windlass in his fleece pocket, and he holds the coffee with both hands.

p1-clive-6.speaker: clive
p1-clive-6.text: A lock is a box of water with a pair of gates at each end. To take a boat up, you bring it into the box while it's empty, shut the bottom gates and wind up the top paddles. The water comes in from the canal above.
p1-clive-6.say: [gentle, precise] A lock is a box of water with a pair of gates at each end. To take a boat up, you bring it into the box while it's empty, shut the bottom gates and wind up the top paddles. The water comes in from the canal above.

p1-clive-7.speaker: clive
p1-clive-7.text: To go down, you do it the other way round. So a boat that goes down leaves the lock empty, and a boat that goes up leaves it full.
p1-clive-7.say: [gentle, precise] To go down, you do it the other way round. So a boat that goes down leaves the lock empty, and a boat that goes up leaves it full.

p1-clive-8.speaker: ros
p1-clive-8.say: [calm, plain] And the water for it?

p1-clive-9.speaker: clive
p1-clive-9.text: From the pound, the stretch of canal between this lock and the next one up. A lock this size holds about sixty tonnes. When it fills, the pound drops.
p1-clive-9.say: [gentle, precise] From the pound, the stretch of canal between this lock and the next one up. A lock this size holds about sixty tonnes. When it fills, the pound drops.

p1-fifteen-1.speaker: narrator
p1-fifteen-1.text: Two hundred metres up the towpath, lock fifteen is empty. Both pairs of gates are shut.
p1-fifteen-1.say: [quiet, observant] Two hundred metres up the towpath, lock fifteen is empty. Both pairs of gates are shut.

p1-fifteen-2.speaker: narrator
p1-fifteen-2.text: Between the two locks the canal is low. A strip of wet brick, a foot high, runs along the bank above the water. The trust's work boat sits on the mud at an angle, its mooring ropes tight.
p1-fifteen-2.say: [quiet, observant] Between the two locks the canal is low. A strip of wet brick, a foot high, runs along the bank above the water. The trust's work boat sits on the mud at an angle, its mooring ropes tight.

p10-1.speaker: narrator
p10-1.text: Monday, half past eight. The coroner's office. Your report is on three sheets, in a card folder, with the index cards from your board clipped to the back.
p10-1.say: [quiet, observant] Monday, half past eight. The coroner's office. Your report is on three sheets, in a card folder, with the index cards from your board clipped to the back.

p10-2.speaker: narrator
p10-2.text: At ten to nine there is a knock. DCI Hester Quaile, in a raincoat. Her hearing aid is on.
p10-2.say: [quiet, observant] At ten to nine there is a knock. DCI Hester Quaile, in a raincoat. Her hearing aid is on.

p10-3.speaker: quaile
p10-3.text: The coroner says you've a file on the canal death that I'll want. I've come to read it before he does.
p10-3.say: [drily] The coroner says you've a file on the canal death that I'll want. I've come to read it before he does.

p10-quaile-1.speaker: narrator
p10-quaile-1.text: Quaile reads the whole file, every sheet and every card, without a word. It takes eleven minutes. Once she turns a card over to see if there is anything on the back.
p10-quaile-1.say: [quiet, observant] Quaile reads the whole file, every sheet and every card, without a word. It takes eleven minutes. Once she turns a card over to see if there is anything on the back.

p10-quaile-2.speaker: quaile
p10-quaile-2.text: One question. The chain on fourteen. Who unlocked it?
p10-quaile-2.say: [drily] One question. The chain on fourteen. Who unlocked it?

p10-quaile-3.speaker: ros
p10-quaile-3.text: It was chained at 23:13; Neville photographed it. To fill the lock someone unlocked it after that. Two of the three keys were in Neville's coat, in the water. The third is Clive Amory's.
p10-quaile-3.say: [calm, plain] It was chained at 23:13; Neville photographed it. To fill the lock someone unlocked it after that. Two of the three keys were in Neville's coat, in the water. The third is Clive Amory's.

p10-quaile-5.speaker: quaile
p10-quaile-5.text: Thinking won't do. His solicitor will ask how.
p10-quaile-5.say: [drily] Thinking won't do. His solicitor will ask how.

p10-quaile-6.speaker: quaile
p10-quaile-6.text: Yes. That's what I'd have asked him.
p10-quaile-6.say: [drily] Yes. That's what I'd have asked him.

p10-quaile-7.speaker: quaile
p10-quaile-7.text: Then his solicitor will say it was never unlocked at all.
p10-quaile-7.say: [drily] Then his solicitor will say it was never unlocked at all.

p2-1.speaker: narrator
p2-1.text: The towpath climbs beside the flight. Sixteen, fifteen and fourteen have their paddle gear chained, each post wrapped in a chain with a brass padlock. Thirteen, below the cottage, is not.
p2-1.say: [quiet, observant] The towpath climbs beside the flight. Sixteen, fifteen and fourteen have their paddle gear chained, each post wrapped in a chain with a brass padlock. Thirteen, below the cottage, is not.

p2-2.speaker: narrator
p2-2.text: The lock cottage is the trust's office, with a flat upstairs for the lock-keeper.
p2-2.say: [quiet, observant] The lock cottage is the trust's office, with a flat upstairs for the lock-keeper.

p2-coat-1.speaker: narrator
p2-coat-1.text: The police have left Neville's coat on a hook, in a clear bag, with a form for you to sign. Wallet. A torch, switched off. A phone, dead from the water. A ring with two small brass keys: one with N.S. scratched on the bow, one with a paper label in round handwriting, K.R.
p2-coat-1.say: [quiet, observant] The police have left Neville's coat on a hook, in a clear bag, with a form for you to sign. Wallet. A torch, switched off. A phone, dead from the water. A ring with two small brass keys: one with N.S. scratched on the bow, one with a paper label in round handwriting, K.R.

p2-coat-2.speaker: narrator
p2-coat-2.text: Above the hook, on the wall, a typed list: Chain keys. N. Strand. C. Amory. K. Rowe.
p2-coat-2.say: [quiet, observant] Above the hook, on the wall, a typed list: Chain keys. N. Strand. C. Amory. K. Rowe.

p2-kit-10.speaker: kit
p2-kit-10.text: He's why I can do this job.
p2-kit-10.say: [flat, quick] He's why I can do this job.

p2-kit-11.speaker: narrator
p2-kit-11.text: She turns the label over. On the back, in the same hand: spare.
p2-kit-11.say: [quiet, observant] She turns the label over. On the back, in the same hand: spare.

p2-kit-12.speaker: kit
p2-kit-12.text: I gave him that at twenty to eight. I had a train.
p2-kit-12.say: [quietly] I gave him that at twenty to eight. I had a train.

p2-kit-13.speaker: kit
p2-kit-13.text: I was in Bristol. Interview at nine on Friday, at Cumberland Basin. Lock-keeper for the Harbour, on the big locks to the river. Neville knew. He said he wouldn't tell the committee.
p2-kit-13.say: [flat, quick] I was in Bristol. Interview at nine on Friday, at Cumberland Basin. Lock-keeper for the Harbour, on the big locks to the river. Neville knew. He said he wouldn't tell the committee.

p2-kit-14.speaker: narrator
p2-kit-14.text: She fetches a train ticket and a letter from the flat: the 19:52 from Kemble on Thursday, and an interview at nine, Friday, signed by the Harbour Master's office.
p2-kit-14.say: [quiet, observant] She fetches a train ticket and a letter from the flat: the 19:52 from Kemble on Thursday, and an interview at nine, Friday, signed by the Harbour Master's office.

p2-kit-15.speaker: kit
p2-kit-15.text: Don't tell Clive. Please. If they know I'm going they'll end the post before I've got the other one.
p2-kit-15.say: [urgent, low] Don't tell Clive. Please. If they know I'm going they'll end the post before I've got the other one.

p2-kit-2.speaker: narrator
p2-kit-2.text: A card is pinned to the door of the flat: AWAY TILL SAT. Kit.
p2-kit-2.say: [quiet, observant] A card is pinned to the door of the flat: AWAY TILL SAT. Kit.

p2-kit-3.speaker: narrator
p2-kit-3.text: Kit Rowe is twenty-four, in a lock-keeper's fleece with the sleeves pushed up. She has a mug in one hand and a windlass hooked in her belt.
p2-kit-3.say: [quiet, observant] Kit Rowe is twenty-four, in a lock-keeper's fleece with the sleeves pushed up. She has a mug in one hand and a windlass hooked in her belt.

p2-kit-4.speaker: ros
p2-kit-4.text: Ros Kettering, coroner's officer. I'm sorry about Mr Strand.
p2-kit-4.say: [calm, plain] Ros Kettering, coroner's officer. I'm sorry about Mr Strand.

p2-kit-6.speaker: ros
p2-kit-6.text: Were you here on Thursday night?
p2-kit-6.say: [calm, plain] Were you here on Thursday night?

p2-kit-7.speaker: kit
p2-kit-7.text: I was here all night. Upstairs. I heard nothing. I sleep with the window shut.
p2-kit-7.say: [flat, quick] I was here all night. Upstairs. I heard nothing. I sleep with the window shut.

p2-kit-8.speaker: kit
p2-kit-8.text: Down leaves it empty, up leaves it full. You fill it from the pound above. Fifteen's slow; the bottom paddles stick.
p2-kit-8.say: [flat, quick] Down leaves it empty, up leaves it full. You fill it from the pound above. Fifteen's slow; the bottom paddles stick.

p2-kit-9.speaker: kit
p2-kit-9.text: He walked the flight every night at ten and wrote down the levels. He knew every lock on the Arm by its sound.
p2-kit-9.say: [flat, quick] He walked the flight every night at ten and wrote down the levels. He knew every lock on the Arm by its sound.

p2-minutes-1.speaker: narrator
p2-minutes-1.text: The minutes of Thursday's committee, in the same round handwriting.
p2-minutes-1.say: [quiet, observant] The minutes of Thursday's committee, in the same round handwriting.

p2-minutes-2.speaker: narrator
p2-minutes-2.text: Item four. The chairman proposed that the paid lock-keeper post end in March. To be discussed in November.
p2-minutes-2.say: [quiet, observant] Item four. The chairman proposed that the paid lock-keeper post end in March. To be discussed in November.

p2-minutes-3.speaker: narrator
p2-minutes-3.text: Item seven, any other business. The chairman will bring something about the gates to the next meeting.
p2-minutes-3.say: [quiet, observant] Item seven, any other business. The chairman will bring something about the gates to the next meeting.

p2-minutes-4.speaker: narrator
p2-minutes-4.text: Under it, in pencil, a drawing of a gate with a face.
p2-minutes-4.say: [quiet, observant] Under it, in pencil, a drawing of a gate with a face.

p3-1.speaker: narrator
p3-1.text: Wren is moored on the lock landing below thirteen, next to a sign that says NO MOORING. A green hire boat, fifty feet long, with geraniums in a tin on the roof. The police have asked the van Dams to stay until Monday.
p3-1.say: [quiet, observant] Wren is moored on the lock landing below thirteen, next to a sign that says NO MOORING. A green hire boat, fifty feet long, with geraniums in a tin on the roof. The police have asked the van Dams to stay until Monday.

p3-joost-10.speaker: joost
p3-joost-10.text: We were afraid it looks like a fight. It was not a fight. He was a man who wants to show you.
p3-joost-10.say: [careful, formal] We were afraid it looks like a fight. It was not a fight. He was a man who wants to show you.

p3-joost-11.speaker: joost
p3-joost-11.text: Then we moored here. I know, it is not allowed. We walked down to the pub, and came back at a quarter to twelve. In the car park by the cottage there was a car, with the lights off. Maaike said, lovers.
p3-joost-11.say: [careful, formal] Then we moored here. I know, it is not allowed. We walked down to the pub, and came back at a quarter to twelve. In the car park by the cottage there was a car, with the lights off. Maaike said, lovers.

p3-joost-2.speaker: narrator
p3-joost-2.text: Joost van Dam is coiling a rope on the roof. He coils it twice.
p3-joost-2.say: [quiet, observant] Joost van Dam is coiling a rope on the roof. He coils it twice.

p3-joost-3.speaker: joost
p3-joost-3.say: [careful, formal] You are from the police?

p3-joost-4.speaker: ros
p3-joost-4.text: From the coroner. I find out how people died.
p3-joost-4.say: [calm, plain] From the coroner. I find out how people died.

p3-joost-5.speaker: joost
p3-joost-5.text: We did not see him after lock fifteen. He shouted at us there, about a paddle. Then we went on, and we did not see him again.
p3-joost-5.say: [careful, formal] We did not see him after lock fifteen. He shouted at us there, about a paddle. Then we went on, and we did not see him again.

p3-joost-6.speaker: joost
p3-joost-6.text: I do not know about this.
p3-joost-6.say: [careful, formal] I do not know about this.

p3-joost-7.speaker: joost
p3-joost-7.text: Yes, it is ours. We lost it somewhere. I do not know where.
p3-joost-7.say: [careful, formal] Yes, it is ours. We lost it somewhere. I do not know where.

p3-joost-8.speaker: narrator
p3-joost-8.text: He looks at the man with the torch on his wife's phone.
p3-joost-8.say: [quiet, observant] He looks at the man with the torch on his wife's phone.

p3-joost-9.speaker: joost
p3-joost-9.text: Yes. At fourteen also. He stood there and told us how to do it. Then he took my windlass, to show me. I took it back from him, and it fell on the stones. In the dark I could not find it.
p3-joost-9.say: [reluctant] Yes. At fourteen also. He stood there and told us how to do it. Then he took my windlass, to show me. I took it back from him, and it fell on the stones. In the dark I could not find it.

p3-maaike-1.speaker: maaike
p3-maaike-1.text: You can have all of them. I will send them.
p3-maaike-1.say: [direct] You can have all of them. I will send them.

p3-maaike-2.speaker: narrator
p3-maaike-2.text: Maaike van Dam opens the hatch before you knock. She has her phone ready.
p3-maaike-2.say: [quiet, observant] Maaike van Dam opens the hatch before you knock. She has her phone ready.

p3-maaike-3.speaker: maaike
p3-maaike-3.text: You want these. I took them for my sister, because the locks are so old.
p3-maaike-3.say: [direct] You want these. I took them for my sister, because the locks are so old.

p3-maaike-4.speaker: narrator
p3-maaike-4.text: Two photographs, by headlamp. 22:38: lock fourteen, nearly empty, the hire boat low in the chamber. 22:41: the lock empty, the boat leaving through the open bottom gates, and on the lockside above, a man in a dark coat with a torch, pointing.
p3-maaike-4.say: [quiet, observant] Two photographs, by headlamp. 22:38: lock fourteen, nearly empty, the hire boat low in the chamber. 22:41: the lock empty, the boat leaving through the open bottom gates, and on the lockside above, a man in a dark coat with a torch, pointing.

p3-maaike-5.speaker: maaike
p3-maaike-5.text: That is him, with the torch. Joost, tell her about the windlass.
p3-maaike-5.say: [direct] That is him, with the torch. Joost, tell her about the windlass.

p3-maaike-6.speaker: narrator
p3-maaike-6.text: Joost, on the roof, does not answer.
p3-maaike-6.say: [quiet, observant] Joost, on the roof, does not answer.

p4-1.speaker: narrator
p4-1.text: The Strands' house is on Mill Lane in Steeple Wyke: a stone semi with a rain gauge on a post in the front garden.
p4-1.say: [quiet, observant] The Strands' house is on Mill Lane in Steeple Wyke: a stone semi with a rain gauge on a post in the front garden.

p4-annette-11.speaker: annette
p4-annette-11.text: He came back from the Navigation at nine. One pint; he always had one. He went out again at ten to ten with the torch.
p4-annette-11.say: [composed, exact] He came back from the Navigation at nine. One pint; he always had one. He went out again at ten to ten with the torch.

p4-annette-12.speaker: annette
p4-annette-12.text: The phone bill's online. I looked last night, because I couldn't sleep. He rang Clive at five to eleven. Two minutes. After that, nothing.
p4-annette-12.say: [composed, exact] The phone bill's online. I looked last night, because I couldn't sleep. He rang Clive at five to eleven. Two minutes. After that, nothing.

p4-annette-14.speaker: narrator
p4-annette-14.text: She opens a laptop on the kitchen table. Neville's phone sent its photographs to his account as he took them. The last three came in at 23:13.
p4-annette-14.say: [quiet, observant] She opens a laptop on the kitchen table. Neville's phone sent its photographs to his account as he took them. The last three came in at 23:13.

p4-annette-15.speaker: narrator
p4-annette-15.text: The first: a cast iron plate on the beam of a lock gate. The new black paint has been scraped off round it. HOLLINS 1987.
p4-annette-15.say: [quiet, observant] The first: a cast iron plate on the beam of a lock gate. The new black paint has been scraped off round it. HOLLINS 1987.

p4-annette-16.speaker: narrator
p4-annette-16.text: The second: two round wooden plugs in the gate timber, painted over, where bolts had been.
p4-annette-16.say: [quiet, observant] The second: two round wooden plugs in the gate timber, painted over, where bolts had been.

p4-annette-17.speaker: narrator
p4-annette-17.text: The third: the plate again, from further back, in the torchlight. Behind it, the paddle post of lock fourteen, with its chain on.
p4-annette-17.say: [quiet, observant] The third: the plate again, from further back, in the torchlight. Behind it, the paddle post of lock fourteen, with its chain on.

p4-annette-18.speaker: annette
p4-annette-18.text: That's fourteen. He was looking at the gates.
p4-annette-18.say: [composed, exact] That's fourteen. He was looking at the gates.

p4-annette-19.speaker: annette
p4-annette-19.text: He kept every receipt. He'd been up in the study every night since the summer.
p4-annette-19.say: [composed, exact] He kept every receipt. He'd been up in the study every night since the summer.

p4-annette-2.speaker: narrator
p4-annette-2.text: Annette Strand is sixty-four, in a cardigan buttoned to the top. She has made tea and not drunk it.
p4-annette-2.say: [quiet, observant] Annette Strand is sixty-four, in a cardigan buttoned to the top. She has made tea and not drunk it.

p4-annette-20.speaker: narrator
p4-annette-20.text: In the study, a box file marked GATES.
p4-annette-20.say: [quiet, observant] In the study, a box file marked GATES.

p4-annette-21.speaker: narrator
p4-annette-21.text: A letter from the heritage grant office in Bristol: £180,000 paid in April for two pairs of new oak gates, locks thirteen and fourteen, maker Hollins and Daughter. The work signed off as complete by C. Amory, treasurer. Pinned to it, in Neville's pencil: Rang Bristol Wed. for maker's certificate. They have none.
p4-annette-21.say: [quiet, observant] A letter from the heritage grant office in Bristol: £180,000 paid in April for two pairs of new oak gates, locks thirteen and fourteen, maker Hollins and Daughter. The work signed off as complete by C. Amory, treasurer. Pinned to it, in Neville's pencil: Rang Bristol Wed. for maker's certificate. They have none.

p4-annette-22.speaker: narrator
p4-annette-22.text: Under it, a statement for the trust's reserve account, with two lines ringed. Two years ago: £150,000 out, to the Meridian Income Fund, authorised C. Amory. This June: £150,000 in, "anonymous donation". In the margin: Meridian closed March 2025.
p4-annette-22.say: [quiet, observant] Under it, a statement for the trust's reserve account, with two lines ringed. Two years ago: £150,000 out, to the Meridian Income Fund, authorised C. Amory. This June: £150,000 in, "anonymous donation". In the margin: Meridian closed March 2025.

p4-annette-3.speaker: annette
p4-annette-3.text: You'll want to know about Thursday.
p4-annette-3.say: [composed, exact] You'll want to know about Thursday.

p4-annette-4.speaker: narrator
p4-annette-4.text: Before the undertaker can ring her, you tell her yourself.
p4-annette-4.say: [quiet, observant] Before the undertaker can ring her, you tell her yourself.

p4-annette-5.speaker: ros
p4-annette-5.text: I've asked the coroner for a second post-mortem. The funeral will have to move.
p4-annette-5.say: [calm, plain] I've asked the coroner for a second post-mortem. The funeral will have to move.

p4-annette-6.speaker: annette
p4-annette-6.text: The undertaker rang. He says there's to be another post-mortem, and the funeral can't be Wednesday. Nobody from your office rang me.
p4-annette-6.say: [cold, controlled] The undertaker rang. He says there's to be another post-mortem, and the funeral can't be Wednesday. Nobody from your office rang me.

p4-annette-7.speaker: ros
p4-annette-7.text: The first post-mortem can't tell if he was awake in the water. The second one can. If he was awake, I need to know how the lock came to be full.
p4-annette-7.say: [calm, plain] The first post-mortem can't tell if he was awake in the water. The second one can. If he was awake, I need to know how the lock came to be full.

p4-annette-9.speaker: ros
p4-annette-9.text: I'm sorry. Someone should have told you first.
p4-annette-9.say: [calm, plain] I'm sorry. Someone should have told you first.

p4-notebook-1.speaker: narrator
p4-notebook-1.text: On the hall table is a small notebook with a pencil in the spine. Annette sees you looking.
p4-notebook-1.say: [quiet, observant] On the hall table is a small notebook with a pencil in the spine. Annette sees you looking.

p4-notebook-2.speaker: annette
p4-notebook-2.text: The water levels. Every lock, every night, for eleven years.
p4-notebook-2.say: [composed, exact] The water levels. Every lock, every night, for eleven years.

p4-notebook-3.speaker: narrator
p4-notebook-3.text: The pages are columns of numbers in pencil. The last entry is Thursday. Lock fifteen. Then the page is blank.
p4-notebook-3.say: [quiet, observant] The pages are columns of numbers in pencil. The last entry is Thursday. Lock fifteen. Then the page is blank.

p5-1.speaker: narrator
p5-1.text: The Navigation Inn, by lock eleven: low beams, a fire, a darts board, a lane up to the lock car park.
p5-1.say: [quiet, observant] The Navigation Inn, by lock eleven: low beams, a fire, a darts board, a lane up to the lock car park.

p5-pete-1.speaker: narrator
p5-pete-1.text: Pete Garrow is behind the bar, drying glasses.
p5-pete-1.say: [quiet, observant] Pete Garrow is behind the bar, drying glasses.

p5-pete-2.speaker: pete
p5-pete-2.text: One pint of Hook Norton, half eight, same as every Thursday. Gone by nine.
p5-pete-2.say: [gruff, unhurried] One pint of Hook Norton, half eight, same as every Thursday. Gone by nine.

p5-pete-3.speaker: pete
p5-pete-3.text: Came in at five past eleven. Two halves of cider and two packets of crisps. Left at twenty to twelve. She paid.
p5-pete-3.say: [gruff, unhurried] Came in at five past eleven. Two halves of cider and two packets of crisps. Left at twenty to twelve. She paid.

p5-pete-4.speaker: pete
p5-pete-4.text: Put the bins out at twenty to twelve. Clive Amory's car was up in the lock car park. Green estate, trust sticker. He leaves it here on quiz nights. Engine off, lights off.
p5-pete-4.say: [gruff, unhurried] Put the bins out at twenty to twelve. Clive Amory's car was up in the lock car park. Green estate, trust sticker. He leaves it here on quiz nights. Engine off, lights off.

p5-pete-5.speaker: pete
p5-pete-5.text: Somebody in it. I didn't look.
p5-pete-5.say: [gruff, unhurried] Somebody in it. I didn't look.

p6-1.speaker: narrator
p6-1.text: The coroner's office in Cirencester, above a solicitor's. Your desk, your kettle, a window on the car park.
p6-1.say: [quiet, observant] The coroner's office in Cirencester, above a solicitor's. Your desk, your kettle, a window on the car park.

p6-sam-2.speaker: narrator
p6-sam-2.text: DS Sam Adeyemi is at the door with a box of pastries from the station.
p6-sam-2.say: [quiet, observant] DS Sam Adeyemi is at the door with a box of pastries from the station.

p6-sam-3.speaker: sam
p6-sam-3.text: The DCI said you'd be in. I'm to tell you there's no crime on our side. A man of sixty-six on a towpath in the dark. I'm sorry.
p6-sam-3.say: [measured, kind] The DCI said you'd be in. I'm to tell you there's no crime on our side. A man of sixty-six on a towpath in the dark. I'm sorry.

p6-sam-4.speaker: ros
p6-sam-4.text: Do you think there's no crime?
p6-sam-4.say: [calm, plain] Do you think there's no crime?

p6-sam-5.speaker: sam
p6-sam-5.text: I think he fell. I'd tell you if I thought he didn't.
p6-sam-5.say: [measured, kind] I think he fell. I'd tell you if I thought he didn't.

p6-sam-6.speaker: narrator
p6-sam-6.say: [quiet, observant] He leaves you the pastries.

p6-shah-1.speaker: narrator
p6-shah-1.text: Dr Shah rings from the mortuary.
p6-shah-1.say: [quiet, observant] Dr Shah rings from the mortuary.

p6-shah-2.speaker: shah
p6-shah-2.text: I've done the second one this morning. I'll ring you tonight, when it's written up.
p6-shah-2.say: [brisk, clinical] I've done the second one this morning. I'll ring you tonight, when it's written up.

p6-shah-3.speaker: narrator
p6-shah-3.text: Dr Imogen Shah rings on the dot of ten. You can hear a station announcer.
p6-shah-3.say: [quiet, observant] Dr Imogen Shah rings on the dot of ten. You can hear a station announcer.

p6-shah-4.speaker: shah
p6-shah-4.text: Neville Strand. Drowning: water in the lungs and airways, froth. In plain words, he breathed water in, so he was alive in it.
p6-shah-4.say: [brisk, clinical] Neville Strand. Drowning: water in the lungs and airways, froth. In plain words, he breathed water in, so he was alive in it.

p6-shah-5.speaker: shah
p6-shah-5.text: Left thigh broken, from a fall onto an edge. A bruise on the back of the head. I can't tell you yet how hard he hit it. Blood alcohol low. About one pint.
p6-shah-5.say: [brisk, clinical] Left thigh broken, from a fall onto an edge. A bruise on the back of the head. I can't tell you yet how hard he hit it. Blood alcohol low. About one pint.

p6-shah-6.speaker: shah
p6-shah-6.text: There's always some water at the bottom of an empty lock, isn't there? Half a metre is enough if you're unconscious. I can't tell you how deep it was.
p6-shah-6.say: [brisk, clinical] There's always some water at the bottom of an empty lock, isn't there? Half a metre is enough if you're unconscious. I can't tell you how deep it was.

p6-shah-7.speaker: shah
p6-shah-7.text: A forensic one. The brain, for the head injury. The hands, the nails. Bruising under the skin. It would tell you whether he was awake.
p6-shah-7.say: [brisk, clinical] A forensic one. The brain, for the head injury. The hands, the nails. Bruising under the skin. It would tell you whether he was awake.

p7-1.speaker: narrator
p7-1.text: The top gate of lock fourteen. The police tape is gone. The new black paint on the balance beam shines.
p7-1.say: [quiet, observant] The top gate of lock fourteen. The police tape is gone. The new black paint on the balance beam shines.

p7-2.speaker: narrator
p7-2.say: [quiet, observant] The top gate of fourteen.

p7-plate-1.speaker: narrator
p7-plate-1.text: At the end of the beam the paint has been scraped back with a blade, in a rough square. Under it is a cast iron plate: HOLLINS 1987.
p7-plate-1.say: [quiet, observant] At the end of the beam the paint has been scraped back with a blade, in a rough square. Under it is a cast iron plate: HOLLINS 1987.

p7-plate-2.speaker: narrator
p7-plate-2.text: Lower down, two round wooden plugs in the timber, painted over, where bolts went through once. There is no ironwork that fits them on this lock.
p7-plate-2.say: [quiet, observant] Lower down, two round wooden plugs in the timber, painted over, where bolts went through once. There is no ironwork that fits them on this lock.

p7-post-1.speaker: narrator
p7-post-1.text: The paddle post has its chain on, and a brass padlock. The square spindle where a windlass fits is bright with new grease. A smear of the same grease is on the chain, at the height of a hand.
p7-post-1.say: [quiet, observant] The paddle post has its chain on, and a brass padlock. The square spindle where a windlass fits is bright with new grease. A smear of the same grease is on the chain, at the height of a hand.

p7-pound-1.speaker: narrator
p7-pound-1.text: The pound to fifteen is still a foot down. The work boat sits on the mud. Fifteen is empty.
p7-pound-1.say: [quiet, observant] The pound to fifteen is still a foot down. The work boat sits on the mud. Fifteen is empty.

p7-pound-2.speaker: narrator
p7-pound-2.text: The pound to fifteen has come back up from the overflow weir at fifteen, and the work boat floats again. Fifteen is still empty, its gates shut and chained.
p7-pound-2.say: [quiet, observant] The pound to fifteen has come back up from the overflow weir at fifteen, and the work boat floats again. Fifteen is still empty, its gates shut and chained.

p9-1.speaker: narrator
p9-1.text: Clive Amory lives in the last house on Wyke Hill, with a view of the whole flight. The green estate is on the drive.
p9-1.say: [quiet, observant] Clive Amory lives in the last house on Wyke Hill, with a view of the whole flight. The green estate is on the drive.

p9-car-1.speaker: narrator
p9-car-1.text: Clive opens the boot. A trust fleece, a first-aid box, wellingtons, and a windlass with a worn wooden grip.
p9-car-1.say: [quiet, observant] Clive opens the boot. A trust fleece, a first-aid box, wellingtons, and a windlass with a worn wooden grip.

p9-car-2.speaker: narrator
p9-car-2.text: The socket of the windlass is packed with fresh grease.
p9-car-2.say: [quiet, observant] The socket of the windlass is packed with fresh grease.

p9-car-3.speaker: clive
p9-car-3.text: I did the paddles on sixteen on Wednesday.
p9-car-3.say: [gentle, precise] I did the paddles on sixteen on Wednesday.

p9-clive-10.speaker: clive
p9-clive-10.text: Reclaimed ironwork, perhaps. A good maker reuses a sound plate, and Ted Hollins is a very good maker. You would have to ask him; I only sign for the work, I don't build it.
p9-clive-10.say: [gentle, precise] Reclaimed ironwork, perhaps. A good maker reuses a sound plate, and Ted Hollins is a very good maker. You would have to ask him; I only sign for the work, I don't build it.

p9-clive-11.speaker: clive
p9-clive-11.text: Every windlass on this canal has grease on it, Mrs Kettering, and every paddle on the flight was greased in the spring. I did sixteen on Wednesday. Fourteen is Kit's job, not mine.
p9-clive-11.say: [gentle, precise] Every windlass on this canal has grease on it, Mrs Kettering, and every paddle on the flight was greased in the spring. I did sixteen on Wednesday. Fourteen is Kit's job, not mine.

p9-clive-12.speaker: narrator
p9-clive-12.say: [quiet, observant] Clive takes his glasses off.

p9-clive-13.speaker: clive
p9-clive-13.text: Yes. I went down, after all. I was worried about him; he'd sounded upset. I drove to the car park and walked to fourteen, and he wasn't there. I sat in the car for a while, in case he came back. Then I came home.
p9-clive-13.say: [gentle, precise] Yes. I went down, after all. I was worried about him; he'd sounded upset. I drove to the car park and walked to fourteen, and he wasn't there. I sat in the car for a while, in case he came back. Then I came home.

p9-clive-14.speaker: clive
p9-clive-14.text: I didn't say so, because it sounds as if I left him there.
p9-clive-14.say: [gentle, precise] I didn't say so, because it sounds as if I left him there.

p9-clive-15.speaker: narrator
p9-clive-15.text: He puts his glasses back on and goes through the three photographs twice: the plate, the plugs, the post with its chain.
p9-clive-15.say: [quiet, observant] He puts his glasses back on and goes through the three photographs twice: the plate, the plugs, the post with its chain.

p9-clive-16.speaker: clive
p9-clive-16.say: [short pause] [quiet] The chairman was very thorough.

p9-clive-17.speaker: clive
p9-clive-17.text: I think I'd like to stop now, Mrs Kettering. Will you see yourself out?
p9-clive-17.say: [gentle, precise] I think I'd like to stop now, Mrs Kettering. Will you see yourself out?

p9-clive-2.speaker: narrator
p9-clive-2.text: Clive opens the door in a cardigan, with his reading glasses pushed up.
p9-clive-2.say: [quiet, observant] Clive opens the door in a cardigan, with his reading glasses pushed up.

p9-clive-3.speaker: clive
p9-clive-3.text: Mrs Kettering. Come in. I've put the trust's accounts out for you; I thought you'd want them. They're in order.
p9-clive-3.say: [gentle, precise] Mrs Kettering. Come in. I've put the trust's accounts out for you; I thought you'd want them. They're in order.

p9-clive-4.speaker: narrator
p9-clive-4.text: They are. Every column adds up. The reserve account is shown at £150,000 in each of the last three years.
p9-clive-4.say: [quiet, observant] They are. Every column adds up. The reserve account is shown at £150,000 in each of the last three years.

p9-clive-5.speaker: clive
p9-clive-5.text: As I said, the chairman rang me at five to eleven, and I told him to ring me in the morning. Then I went to bed.
p9-clive-5.say: [gentle, precise] As I said, the chairman rang me at five to eleven, and I told him to ring me in the morning. Then I went to bed.

p9-clive-6.speaker: narrator
p9-clive-6.text: He takes his car keys from his pocket. With them is a small brass key with C.A. scratched on the bow.
p9-clive-6.say: [quiet, observant] He takes his car keys from his pocket. With them is a small brass key with C.A. scratched on the bow.

p9-clive-7.speaker: clive
p9-clive-7.text: Always. The chairman was very particular about the keys.
p9-clive-7.say: [gentle, precise] Always. The chairman was very particular about the keys.

p9-clive-8.speaker: clive
p9-clive-8.text: Hollins and Daughter. Ted Hollins is a craftsman; I was at school with him. Oak, from a French forest, seasoned four years. I can show you the invoice. It's in the file.
p9-clive-8.say: [gentle, precise] Hollins and Daughter. Ted Hollins is a craftsman; I was at school with him. Oak, from a French forest, seasoned four years. I can show you the invoice. It's in the file.

p9-clive-9.speaker: clive
p9-clive-9.text: Meridian was a mistake, and it was mine; the committee approved the investment, and the fund failed, as funds do. The gift in June came from someone who loves this canal and wants no thanks for it, and I have respected that, as I'd respect it from anyone.
p9-clive-9.say: [gentle, precise] Meridian was a mistake, and it was mine; the committee approved the investment, and the fund failed, as funds do. The gift in June came from someone who loves this canal and wants no thanks for it, and I have respected that, as I'd respect it from anyone.

q-alive-1.speaker: narrator
q-alive-1.text: He fell into an empty lock and broke his leg. He breathed water in, so he was alive in it. Someone filled the lock.
q-alive-1.say: [quiet, observant] He fell into an empty lock and broke his leg. He breathed water in, so he was alive in it. Someone filled the lock.

q-alive-2.speaker: narrator
q-alive-2.text: Dr Shah's second report: he was awake, and he could have sat up in the water at the bottom. He drowned because someone made it deeper.
q-alive-2.say: [quiet, observant] Dr Shah's second report: he was awake, and he could have sat up in the water at the bottom. He drowned because someone made it deeper.

q-alive-3.speaker: narrator
q-alive-3.text: If he was knocked out, he could have drowned in the water at the bottom of an empty lock. If he was awake, he drowned because someone filled it. Only a second post-mortem can say which.

q-chain-1.speaker: narrator
q-chain-1.text: At 23:13 the paddle gear on fourteen was chained. To fill the lock, someone had to unlock it after that. A padlock snaps shut without a key, so the chain on it at dawn proves nothing. The unlocking does. There are three keys. Two were in Neville's pocket, in the water.

q-filled-1.speaker: narrator
q-filled-1.text: The hire boat came down the flight last night, through fifteen and fourteen, and left both empty. A boat coming up would have filled fourteen and then had to fill fifteen. Fifteen is still empty. So nobody came up. Someone wound the paddles on fourteen by hand, and the water came out of the pound.
